conflict_topics: claiming a seat via an item (tissue packet) as a reservation
timing for finishing a meal vs. another's limited waiting time
who may take an alternative seat
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants give concrete practical reasons (time remaining to eat, bowl fullness, aisle blocking).
Alex repeats his four-minute waiting limit across multiple turns ('I can only wait up to four minutes'), a small amount of reiteration but contextually relevant.
Robin's physical action (TAKE_SEAT) is a clear, well-timed de-escalating move.
Casey contributes a practical constraint (standing would block aisle) that helps frame feasible accommodations.
evaluation.final_reason: Jamie finished the bowl and vacated the disputed seat; Alex took the seat and Robin had already taken the nearby alternative seat, so the incompatible demands were removed by Jamie leaving (accommodation of Alex's need).
position_change_notes: Jamie held to her position (would not stand or yield) until her bowl was finished, then vacated the seat — clear conditional change tied to finishing the meal (Turn 4, Turn 10, LEAVE_SEAT).
Alex consistently asserted a reservation claim and a four-minute waiting limit and maintained that position until he took the seat (Turns 1, 7, 9; TAKE_SEAT).
Robin shifted from a third-party claimant to occupying the alternative seat (Turn 6; TAKE_SEAT), thereby removing one element of competition.
Casey did not change a seat-related position; provided a single practical objection about blocking the aisle (Turn 3).

round_scores.evidence: Alex claims the tissue packet as a reservation and demands Jamie move within four minutes; Jamie rejects that automatic priority and says she needs eight minutes to finish the bowl (Turns 1–2). Incompatible demands over the same seat are explicit and unresolved.

Two minutes pass with no movement. Jamie refuses to stand (would block aisle) and reiterates she will move only when the bowl is empty, still needing about six minutes; Alex's demand to be seated within four minutes remains (Public update; Turns 3–4).

Another standing party (Robin) enters the contest, citing Alex's packet and saying they'll take the next genuinely empty seat; Alex reiterates his four-minute limit and asks Jamie not to relinquish the seat to Robin (Public update; Turns 6–7). The disagreement now involves an additional stakeholder, increasing contestation.

An alternative seat appears and Robin takes it (Observable action). Jamie has only several spoonfuls left. Alex repeats his reservation claim and asks for a concrete accommodation (Turn 9). The entry of a concrete alternative (Robin occupying the other free seat) reduces pressure but the core incompatibility (Jamie occupying the disputed seat while Alex needs to sit now) remains.

Jamie announces she is done and leaves the seat (Turn 10; Observable action), and Alex immediately takes the disputed seat (Observable action). The substantive conflict over who occupies the seat is affirmatively settled by Jamie vacating and Alex taking it.
Two minutes later the confirmed state shows Alex occupying the disputed seat and no standing seat-seekers; no further substantive disagreement is expressed (Public update).

substantive_insights: Informal reservation signals (tissue packet) can be contested and are not authoritative without social acceptance.
Time constraints are the key trade-off: Alex's limited waiting window vs. Jamie's need to finish the bowl.
The presence and choices of a third party (Robin) change leverage and can de-escalate competition by taking alternatives.
Affirmative physical actions (taking or leaving a seat) ultimately resolved the dispute rather than formal bargaining.
